person.name: Maya Chen
person.headline: I build clear, usable websites and product interfaces.
person.intro: I'm a frontend developer working with small product teams. I enjoy turning a well-defined problem into a responsive interface that people can understand and use with confidence.
person.availability: Open to frontend roles and small website projects. Remote within Canada or hybrid in Ottawa.
person.contactCopy: Have a frontend role or a small website project in mind? The fictional contact address is shown here for context. This preview does not send messages.
about: I came to frontend development through maintaining a community newsletter website. I liked the mix of careful implementation and small decisions that make a page easier to use.
My recent work has focused on forms, content-heavy pages and component libraries. I like collaborating with designers, documenting tradeoffs and leaving code that another developer can pick up.
Away from the screen, I enjoy cooking, neighbourhood walks and sketching buildings. I'm currently practising accessible form patterns and learning more about browser performance tools.

projects.title: Cedar Classes
projects.summary: A community studio website that makes class descriptions, schedules and booking information easy to find.
projects.role: Frontend development and content structure, personal demonstration project
projects.problem: The fictional studio's class details were scattered across long pages, so a visitor had to hunt for the time, skill level and materials list.
projects.approach: I grouped classes into a consistent card structure and gave each class a detail section with its schedule, prerequisites and supplies. The small-screen navigation keeps the class list one tap away.
projects.result: The completed demonstration includes six class pages, responsive navigation and a local booking enquiry preview. There is no live booking service or measured conversion result.
projects.learning: Writing the content structure before choosing a layout helped keep the cards consistent without hiding useful detail.
projects.linksNote: This local case study is the available project material. A hosted demo and public repository are not available.

projects.title: Stockroom Notes
projects.summary: A small inventory interface for recording supplies and flagging items that need attention.
projects.problem: A fictional workshop needed a readable way to review stock counts without presenting every editing control at once.
projects.approach: I built a searchable table with clear stock states and a focused edit panel. Form labels, validation and keyboard focus were treated as part of the interface from the start.
projects.result: The prototype supports searching, editing local sample records and reviewing low-stock items. It has no backend, production users or published performance measurements.
projects.learning: Keeping the edit panel focused on one record made error messages easier to explain and test.
projects.linksNote: Read this local case study. The original prototype and its source are not publicly available.

projects.title: Fieldwork Journal
projects.summary: A reading-focused website for a fictional independent design journal.
projects.role: Frontend development from a self-written brief
projects.problem: The journal needed an article template that could handle short announcements and longer essays without separate layouts for every story.
projects.approach: I created a shared reading layout, article metadata and related-story links, then checked headings and line length at narrow and wide widths.
projects.result: The static demonstration contains an issue index and four sample articles. It is a portfolio exercise, with no audience or engagement figures claimed.
projects.learning: A restrained template gave the writing room and made inconsistent spacing much easier to spot.
projects.linksNote: The case study on this page is the supplied record. No external publication or repository link is available.
